unit.title: Goals and limits: a model, linear programming in 2D

lesson.title: Tell the computer
lesson.subtitle: Your first model in Python, and a solver that searches

video.title: Tell the computer
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — your computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talks to the student)

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds the garden graph; behind him a giant timetable grid full of sticky notes.
scenes.animation: The graph shrinks; the timetable grid grows.
scenes.narration: You drew the garden on graph paper: two variables, three lines. Our school timetable has hundreds of choices. Nobody can draw that. So today, you’ll tell a computer instead.

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the Optimization track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: tell the computer, with your first model in Python.

scenes.visual: A phone and a laptop side by side showing the same code; arrows into a gear labelled solver.
scenes.animation: Code appears on both screens; the gear turns.
scenes.narration: Google’s free toolkit, OR-Tools, has a solver that searches for you. You write the model: the variables, the limits and the goal. The solver finds the best plan. It runs small models right here on your phone, and the same program runs on big computers.

scenes.visual: The code card types out four lines.
scenes.animation: Lines type in; the variable lines glow.
scenes.narration: First, make a model and its variables. Each one is a whole number of beds, from zero to ten.

scenes.visual: The code card types out three limits and the goal.
scenes.animation: Lines type in one by one.
scenes.narration: Each limit is one line, just like on paper. Then the goal: make thirty x plus forty y as big as possible.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma points at the line model.add(x + y <= 8). Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! What does this line say: model dot add, x plus y, less than or equal to eight?

scenes.visual: The answer card gets a check; the two signs appear with their words.
scenes.animation: Check pops; the signs slide in.
scenes.narration: x plus y is at most eight: no more than eight beds in all. Read less than or equal as at most. And read greater than or equal as at least.

scenes.visual: The code card types the solve lines; the output appears under it.
scenes.animation: Lines type in; the output slides up.
scenes.narration: Then the solver solves the model, and you print the answer. It prints three and five: the same corner you drew.

scenes.visual: Two status badges: green OPTIMAL, red INFEASIBLE.
scenes.animation: Badges stamp in as each is named.
scenes.narration: The solver also tells you what it found. OPTIMAL means the best plan. INFEASIBLE means no plan keeps every rule: you asked for the impossible.

scenes.visual: A class list beside the garden; one class has no bed; a new rule line is typed into the model.
scenes.animation: The empty class blinks; the new line types in.
scenes.narration: The solver obeys only the rules you write. If every class should get a bed, write it as a rule. If you forget, the solver won’t remind you.

scenes.visual: A phone with the lab: a Python editor with the timetable example, a Run button and the printed timetable.
scenes.animation: A finger taps Run; a new line is typed; the timetable changes.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: Model it with CP-SAT
scenes.narration: In the app, open the timetable example and press Run. Then add one rule: class five A has art in period four. Run it again, and watch the timetable rearrange itself.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph’s phone shows INFEASIBLE in red. Three answer cards appear.
scenes.narration: Your turn. The solver prints INFEASIBLE. What does that mean?

scenes.visual: The answer card gets the check; four summary lines and a takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: No plan keeps all the rules: one rule has to change. Remember: variables, limits and a goal, then solve. Less than or equal means at most. And the solver only knows what you tell it.

scenes.visual: A pupil at home with a phone: the truck example, the number changed, a guess written on paper.
scenes.animation: The number changes; Run; a tick appears next to the guess.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: in the modeller lab, open the truck example. Change the capacity to eleven hundred, and guess what changes before you run it. Were you right?

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — <= means less than or equal to: no more than 8 beds in all.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — <= means less than or equal to, so x + y can be 8 or less: at most 8 beds.

checkpoints.prompt: The solver prints INFEASIBLE. What does that mean?

options.text: No plan keeps all the rules

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — INFEASIBLE means the rules can’t all be kept at once, and the solver has proved it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — INFEASIBLE isn’t a typo or a slow phone. It means no plan keeps every rule, so one rule has to change.
